title: A German Movie Previews Its Far-Right Future
gist: Paul Hockenos uses Faraz Shariat's thriller Prosecution (Staatsschutz) to argue that far-right networks have penetrated German justice and security institutions, which are 'blind in the right eye', without ever being voted in. The AfD's 44% result in Saxony-Anhalt in September 2026 could now hand it formal control of police, prosecutors, and the state intelligence agency.

themes.theme: AfD electoral breakthrough and state capture

insights.claim: The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won 44 percent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt in September 2026 and then 38 percent in another eastern state two weeks later; the author calls these votes seismic events in postwar Germany.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: AfD-led state governments would be a major German political-risk event, affecting investment climate, labor migration, and EU cohesion in eastern Germany.
insights.quote: racked up 44 percent of the vote in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt in September

insights.claim: An AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt holding the justice and interior ministries would control the Staatsschutz, police personnel and priorities, asylum and deportation rules, prosecutors' instructions, and the state intelligence agency, which currently classifies the AfD as 'right-wing extremist'.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: Control of the security apparatus would let the AfD change how its own extremist classification is handled. Watch coalition and ministry allocations.

insights.claim: Many people on the far right's 'undesirable' list in Saxony-Anhalt are reportedly sitting on packed bags, and the author expects conditions for people of color and LGBTQ people to be distinctly worse under the AfD.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: Emigration of minorities and skilled workers from eastern German states would deepen labor shortages there.

insights.so_what: Rising hate-crime risk in AfD-run regions could hit their attractiveness to foreign investors and workers.

themes.theme: Institutional infiltration: 'blind in the right eye'

insights.claim: The author argues the far right has crept into German institutions without being voted in. German media regularly report far-right chat groups in police units, neo-Nazi cliques in the armed forces, and AfD-affiliated judges and prosecutors.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: Weak institutional resistance raises the risk that elected AfD governments meet little internal pushback.
insights.quote: the far right has crept into German institutions without ever being voted into them
insights.locator: Prosecution is all the more chilling

insights.claim: According to interior ministry statistics, right-wing extremists committed 42,544 crimes in Germany in 2025, including 8,396 explicitly xenophobic hate crimes. Critics suspect the true numbers are much higher.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: This hard baseline of far-right crime can be tracked for escalation in 2026 statistics.
insights.locator: Prosecution is all the more chilling

insights.claim: Critics like Shariat charge that racist hate crimes are often not prosecuted or are treated as apolitical, which hides a potent fascist network running across all of Germany, not just the former East.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: This is a contrarian corrective to the view that the far-right problem is limited to the East.
insights.quote: a potent fascist network runs across the country, in all directions, not just in former East Germany
insights.locator: Racist hate crimes, critics like Shariat

insights.claim: The NSU neo-Nazi cell murdered a policewoman and nine people of primarily Turkish background between 2000 and 2007. Authorities targeted the victims' families and blamed Turkish organized crime, and identified the killers only after finding an NSU video claiming responsibility.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: It is a historical precedent for systemic institutional failure against far-right terror.

insights.claim: The author argues that the German state protects above all itself, its institutions, personnel, and reputation, so it has no interest in making federal cases out of racist and neo-Nazi crimes.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: This explains the under-enforcement as reputational self-protection, a pattern likely to persist.

insights.claim: A wave of sharply edged German films picks up the socially critical tradition of 1970s New German Cinema, overturning the image of Germany as a nation of peaceniks. The author says the far right's September election results suggest the country may grow darker still.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: Culture is a leading indicator of domestic political mood.

insights.claim: Faraz Shariat's Prosecution won three prizes at the Berlinale in February 2026 and was called 'a film of the political moment'. It follows a Korean-German prosecutor who is firebombed after reprimanding a neo-Nazi and who uncovers a far-right network inside the justice and security organs.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: Critical acclaim suggests elite cultural anxiety about the far right in Germany.

insights.claim: In Prosecution, a senior prosecutor tells the protagonist that 80 percent of cases like hers go unsolved. The author stresses that Germany's far right includes educated professionals who 'wear ties, drive Porsches, possess law degrees', not only street thugs.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: The far right's reach into the professional class broadens its governing capacity.
insights.quote: Germany’s far right wear ties, drive Porsches, possess law degrees.

insights.claim: Pawel Pawlikowski's Fatherland, about Thomas Mann's 1949 tour of both Germanys, suggests that the postwar state's 'birth defects', such as West German institutions stocked with former Nazis, still resonate today.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: This frames the AfD's rise as rooted in unresolved postwar continuity rather than a sudden shock.
